title: Workplace Safety Behavioral Tendencies in Highway Maintenance: Development of a Content-Valid Item Pool Based on a Dual-Process Framework
abstract: Highway maintenance work exposes employees to persistent safety demands involving live traffic, temporary traffic control, heavy equipment, variable weather, fatigue, and production pressure. The present study reports Phase 1 of a systematic post-exploratory refinement program for a context-specific item pool assessing safety-related behavioral tendencies. A provisional 36-item pool representing seven hypothesized dimensions was evaluated by 10 subject matter experts (SMEs) for relevance and clarity and then examined through cognitive interviews with 6 highway maintenance workers. Item-level content validity indices (I-CVI) ranged from .80 to 1.00 (S-CVI/Ave = .98), and mean item clarity was 3.29 on a 4-point scale. The SME decision audit classified 22 items for retention, 11 for revision, and 3 for removal; subsequent cognitive-interview and readability review produced additional wording refinements, yielding a 33-item revised pool. The near-ceiling relevance profile is interpreted cautiously because 5 of 10 SMEs were drawn from highway maintenance organizations and many panelists shared overlapping safety credentials. Cognitive interviews identified wording clarity and socially desirable phrasing as the most common interpretive problems. The resulting pool remains developmental and is prepared for subsequent psychometric testing; no new claims of reliability, factor structure, predictive validity, or operational use are made for the revised 33-item version.

title: Unveiling the mysteries: neuroprotective potential of Mucuna monosperma seeds in combating haloperidol induced Parkinsonism
journal: Journal of Complementary and Integrative Medicine
abstract: Abstract Objectives Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor dysfunction and loss of dopaminergic neurons. Oxidative stress, defined as detrimental imbalance between free radicals and body’s defense mechanism, is a critical contributing factor. This study evaluated the neuroprotective and antioxidant properties of methanolic extract of Mucuna monosperma seeds (MMMS) in haloperidol induced rat model of PD. Methods PD was induced in rats by intraperitoneal administration of haloperidol (HPD, D 2 blocker) at 1 mg/kg for 21 days. MMMS was administered orally at 100, 200, and 400 mg/kg. Motor abilities were assessed using the catalepsy bar test, actophotometer test, and rotarod test. Biochemical assessments measured markers of oxidative stress, and brain dopamine levels. Histopathological analysis was used to evaluate neuronal integrity. Results Motor abilities were tested weekly for 21 days, followed by biochemical and histological analysis. HPD caused motor deficits, raised oxidative stress, and lowered dopamine. MMMS (400 mg/kg) improved motor function by decreasing catalepsy, increasing locomotion, and prolonging rotarod time (p < 0.0001). It also reduced oxidative stress, nearly normalized dopamine. Also, the levels of endogenous antioxidants like glutathione (GSH), super oxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT) are also boosted and reduction of malonaldehyde (MDA), indicator of lipid peroxidation which may help in prevention of degradation of dopaminergic neurons. Histology showed better neuron preservation in MMMS rats. Conclusions This study found MMMS is neuroprotective in HPD-induced PD. Its effects likely stem from antioxidant properties, and dopamine restoration. MMMS may merit further research for PD management.

title: Unpacking innovation at the global level: insights from a systematic review
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to provide an integrated framework while explaining the dynamic relationships among actors, innovation subsystems and system-level structures of different components and levels of the global innovation process by identifying its different characteristics and dimensions. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a systematic literature review of 47 conceptually relevant publications identified through a structured search strategy, complemented by backward reference tracking. A three-stage qualitative coding procedure (initial, intermediate and advanced coding) was applied to synthesize concepts across the actor, subsystem and system levels and to identify higher-order analytical mechanisms underpinning global innovation processes. Findings The findings suggest three primary levels of analysis for the conceptualization of the global innovation process: the actor-level components of the global innovation value network, which include the typology of upstream and downstream actors in the value chain and specific actors of the value network (leaders, systemic intermediaries and champions); sub-system-level components that each have their boundaries, resources, interactions and distinct technological infrastructure; global-level components that include systemic features and include mission orientation, flexibility, complexity and evolution. In addition, the review identifies a set of higher-order cross-cutting mechanisms, including knowledge dynamics, innovation ecosystem governance, structural coupling and global value chain governance, that connect these analytical levels and explain the evolution of global innovation processes. Originality/value This study develops an integrated explanatory framework that connects actors, innovation subsystems and system-level characteristics through a set of higher-order analytical mechanisms. By synthesizing recent developments in global innovation research, including ecosystem governance, knowledge dynamics, structural coupling and global value chain interactions, the framework advances a more comprehensive understanding of how global innovation emerges, evolves and creates value across multiple geographical and institutional contexts.

title: Understanding what retains patients in rheumatic heart disease care: a qualitative study of an integrated control program in northern Uganda
Understanding co-payment for COVID-19 vaccines during period vaccine scarcity: evidence from urban Ghana
abstract: Purpose This study investigates citizens' willingness to pay (WTP) as a complementary financing mechanism for COVID-19 vaccines in Ghana, analyzing behavior during a period of peak prevalence and severe vaccine scarcity. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 2,010 respondents was conducted in the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area. A two-stage regression approach was employed, using a logit model to analyze the decision to pay and ordinary least squares to determine the factors influencing the amount willing to be paid. The analysis integrated Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) and included heterogeneity assessments by gender and age. The two-stage Heckman, double-hurdle and quantile regression models were employed to test the robustness of the WTP results. Findings The study reveals that a significant segment (23%) of the urban population was willing to pay for COVID-19 vaccines during a period of scarcity, with an average amount of GH₵122 (US$24). The decision to pay was primarily driven by attitudinal factors aligned with PMT. However, heterogeneity analysis reveals critical nuances: the drivers of WTP differed markedly by gender and age. A key finding is the role of altruism, where married males with larger families were willing to pay significantly higher amounts, demonstrating that familial protection motives can override individual cost barriers. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design captures WTP at a specific, high-stakes moment, which may not reflect preferences in a non-crisis context. The focus on an urban epicenter population, while methodologically sound for the research questions, limits the generalizability of findings to rural areas. Furthermore, the reliance on stated, rather than revealed, preferences for WTP may be subject to social desirability or hypothetical bias. Practical implications Policymakers should consider demographically sensitive co-payment schemes and tailored public health communication. For long-term resilience, investing in domestic pharmaceutical production is necessary. Originality/value This study provides unique insights by analyzing WTP during an acute vaccine shortage. It moves beyond sociodemographics by integrating behavioral theory and a crucial heterogeneity analysis, offering a nuanced theoretical and practical contribution to sustainable vaccine financing.

title: The bigger picture
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to review the latest management developments across the globe and pinpoint practical implications from cutting-edge research and case studies. Design/methodology/approach This briefing is prepared by an independent writer who adds their own impartial comments and places the articles in context. Findings This paper identified that the more that organizations use GenAI the stronger their online presence would be. This can be useful for smaller organizations so they can invest for their business performance. Originality/value The briefing saves busy executives, strategists and researchers hours of reading time by selecting only the very best, most pertinent information and presenting it in a condensed and easy-to-digest format.

title: Teachers as SDG gatekeepers: educator roles in Sustainable Development Goal integration among secondary students in Lebanon and Dubai
journal: International Journal of Comparative Education and Development
abstract: Purpose This study explores how teachers and school leaders influence secondary school students' engagement with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in Lebanon and Dubai, UAE. Although the two contexts share a regional setting, they differ significantly in their institutional capacity to support sustainability education. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods approach was used. Quantitative data were collected through a survey of 267 Lebanese secondary school students. In Dubai, qualitative data came from focus group discussions with 30 students in three international schools. Semi-structured interviews were also conducted with 11 education professionals across both contexts. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests and inductive thematic coding. Findings The results show a clear structural difference between the two contexts. In Lebanon, sustainability education was described by participants as depending largely on individual teacher or school leadership initiatives. Where such initiative was absent, participants reported that the topic was less likely to be raised in class. In Dubai, participants described sustainability as already present through several national and institutional frameworks before it reached the classroom; the focus group discussions showed high self-reported SDG awareness and strong thematic engagement with Gender Equality and Climate Action among focus group participants. However, both contexts show a gap between awareness and practice: only 28.5% of Lebanese survey respondents reported practising sustainability outside school, and responsible consumption was the least prominently raised theme in the Dubai focus group discussions. Research limitations/implications The study has several limitations. The Dubai qualitative sample consists of 30 students drawn exclusively from internationally oriented schools, limiting statistical generalisability and representativeness of the broader UAE educational system. A methodological asymmetry exists between the two contexts: Lebanon is represented by quantitative survey data while Dubai is represented by qualitative focus group findings; direct numerical comparisons should therefore be read with caution. Data collection was disrupted by COVID-19 in both contexts. Future research should conduct parallel educator-focused studies across both countries and examine how the awareness-action gap evolves as national sustainability initiatives continue to develop. Practical implications Lebanon requires three structural changes: formal SDG integration into the national curriculum, discipline-specific teacher professional development, and stronger civil society and private-sector partnerships to connect sustainability content to students' lived realities. Where the state cannot provide this infrastructure, coordinated multi-stakeholder approaches offer a viable alternative. Dubai's challenge is different. High awareness exists but behavioural change lags, particularly around responsible consumption. Schools need pedagogical approaches that move beyond institutional knowledge delivery toward structured critical reflection, helping students examine the tension between sustainability understanding and everyday lifestyle patterns. In both contexts, systemic reform matters more than individual teacher initiative. Social implications When sustainability education depends on individual educators rather than institutional frameworks, access becomes unequal. In Lebanon, students encounter SDG content largely based on which school they attend and whether a motivated teacher is present. When that individual leaves, the learning disappears with them. This produces not only a curriculum gap but an equity challenge, as confirmed by the biographical educator profiles in Table 4. In Dubai, coordinated national frameworks reduce that inequality but do not eliminate the gap between awareness and behaviour, particularly around consumption. Across both contexts, consumption-driven lifestyles remain the most stubborn barrier to meaningful sustainability practice among young people. Originality/value The study provides a comparative institutional perspective on SDG education in two contrasting Middle East and North Africa (MENA) contexts. It proposes a provisional conceptual distinction between the educator as gatekeeper, characteristic of fragile institutional environments where sustainability education depends on individual initiative, and the system as amplifier, characteristic of contexts with established policy frameworks. Presented as an interpretation generated from these cases rather than a validated model, this framework offers a transferable lens for understanding how institutional capacity shapes SDG education across the Arab world and other resource-constrained settings.

title: Socio-technical TQM configurations and technological innovation ambidexterity: balanced and combined pathways
journal: International Journal of Quality & Reliability Management
abstract: Purpose This study examines how different configurations of social and technical total quality management (TQM) practices shape technological innovation ambidexterity (TIA). Specifically, it distinguishes between balanced and combined TQM practices configurations and investigates their effects on balanced and combined forms of TIA. Design/methodology/approach A configurational framework grounded in socio-technical systems theory and organizational ambidexterity theory was tested using survey data from 113 ISO 9001-certified Tunisian manufacturing firms. The hypotheses were assessed using PLS-SEM. Findings Combined TQM practice configurations positively affect combined TIA but negatively affect balanced TIA. Balanced TQM practice configurations have no significant effect on either form of TIA. These findings indicate that the strong joint development of social and technical TQM practices supports innovation intensity rather than innovation balance. Research limitations/implications The study is limited by its cross-sectional design and its focus on a single-country manufacturing sample. It contributes to the TQM literature by showing that the effect of TQM on innovation depends on the configuration of social and technical TQM practices and on the specific form of ambidexterity considered. Practical implications Managers should configure TQM practices in line with their innovation objectives. Firms seeking high levels of both exploratory and exploitative innovation should strengthen social and technical TQM practices jointly. By contrast, firms seeking a balance between exploration and exploitation should guard against the control bias that may accompany intensive quality systems. Originality/value The study moves beyond linear views of the TQM-innovation relationship by showing that socio-technical TQM configurations differentially shape balanced and combined technological innovation ambidexterity.

title: Research on the Impact of Data Element Agglomeration on Urban Energy Efficiency
abstract: Data elements, as a new type of production factor, inject new momentum into enhancing urban energy efficiency and hold significant importance for achieving China's energy conservation, emission reduction, and green development goals. Based on panel data from 280 prefecture-level cities in China from 2011 to 2023, this study empirically examines the relationship between data element agglomeration and urban energy efficiency using a multi-period difference-in-differences model. The findings reveal that data element agglomeration significantly enhances urban energy efficiency. Mechanism tests indicate that data element agglomeration improves urban energy efficiency by promoting energy-saving technological progress and optimizing energy allocation. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the effect of data element agglomeration on urban energy efficiency is more pronounced in cities where officials have long-term performance perspectives, environmental regulations are stringent, and in resource-based cities. Further analysis demonstrates that data element agglomeration has a positive spatial spillover effect on urban energy efficiency, with the optimal spillover range observed within 200KM to 650KM from the city. This study provides important insights for governments to improve data element institutions and formulate energy conservation and emission reduction policies.
